meanings.short: Symmetry about an axis: the quantity stays the same as you turn around that axis, so it does not depend on the angle φ.
meanings.long: With the axis along z, the azimuthal angle φ measures the turn around it. A potential with azimuthal symmetry depends only on r and θ, and its angular part is a sum of Legendre polynomials in cos θ.

meanings.short: Of a matrix or tensor: having a trace of zero, so that the entries on its main diagonal add up to zero.
meanings.long: For a tensor with more indices, traceless means that setting any two indices equal and summing over them gives zero. Traceless symmetric tensors give the spherical harmonics in 8.07, and in general relativity the Weyl tensor is the traceless part of the curvature.

meanings.short: A tensor that is unchanged when any two of its indices swap places and gives zero when any two are set equal and summed.
meanings.long: Guth uses them in place of the special functions of the textbooks: a traceless symmetric tensor with ℓ indices, multiplied by ℓ copies of the unit vector n̂ and summed, gives a function of direction that solves the angular part of Laplace's equation. Such a tensor has 2ℓ + 1 independent components, as many as the spherical harmonics of degree ℓ.

meanings.short: What is left of a tensor after averaging it over every order of its indices and then removing all its traces.
meanings.long: Guth writes it with curly brackets. For two indices it is simple: the traceless symmetric part of ẑᵢẑⱼ is ẑᵢẑⱼ − δᵢⱼ/3. Multiplied by copies of n̂, the traceless symmetric parts of products of ẑ give numbers times the Legendre polynomials of cos θ.

meanings.short: A rotation that turns the object itself while the coordinate axes stay where they are.
meanings.long: In a passive rotation the coordinate axes turn instead and the object stays still; turning the axes one way changes the components exactly as turning the object the other way would. Guth finds the active picture easier to visualise.

meanings.short: Of light or particles: to be knocked off their path into new directions by something they meet, such as an electron, atom or nucleus.
meanings.long: Sunlight shakes the electrons in air molecules, which radiate the light again in other directions; blue light is scattered most, which is why the sky is blue. How likely a particle is to scatter is measured by a cross-section, an effective target area.

meanings.short: The spread of measured values about their average or about a trend; a large scatter means individual cases differ widely.
The force a charged particle feels from its own radiation, proportional to how fast its acceleration is changing.
meanings.long: It is μ₀q²/(6πc) times the rate of change of the acceleration. Over a cycle of periodic motion it removes exactly the energy the Larmor formula says is radiated, but it also allows runaway solutions, a sign that classical electrodynamics is reaching its limits.

meanings.short: A symbol with indices that is +1 for an even reordering of 1, 2, 3, −1 for an odd one, and 0 if two repeat.
meanings.long: In three dimensions εᵢⱼₖ is +1 for (1, 2, 3) and its cyclic shifts, −1 for the other three orders, and 0 otherwise. It writes the cross product as (A × B)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖAⱼBₖ. In general relativity it is a tensor density rather than a true tensor.

meanings.short: A symbol with two indices that equals 1 when the two indices are the same and 0 when they differ.
meanings.long: δᵢⱼ lists the entries of the identity matrix. Summed against a repeated index it simply renames it: δᵢⱼAⱼ = Aᵢ. The dot products of orthonormal basis vectors are êᵢ · êⱼ = δᵢⱼ.

meanings.short: A choice of the electromagnetic potentials that makes the scalar and vector potentials obey the same wave equation, with charges and currents as sources.
meanings.long: The condition is ∇ · A = −(1/c²) ∂V/∂t. It treats space and time alike, so it suits relativity. It is named after Ludvig Lorenz, not Hendrik Lorentz, though it is often spelled with a t.

meanings.short: In linearized gravity: a choice of coordinates that makes the trace-reversed metric perturbation obey a wave equation, by analogy with electromagnetism.
meanings.long: The condition is that the divergence of the trace-reversed perturbation h̄ vanishes. Einstein's equation then becomes a wave equation with the energy and momentum of matter as its source. Hughes, like many authors, calls it Lorentz gauge.

meanings.short: Writing the far field of a charge or mass distribution as a sum of simpler terms that fade ever faster with distance.
meanings.long: For the potential, the terms are the monopole (set by the total charge, falling as 1/r), the dipole (1/r²), the quadrupole (1/r³) and so on. Far from the source only the first few matter, so a handful of numbers describes even a complicated object.

meanings.short: Splitting a pattern on the sky into standard patterns of ever smaller angular size, numbered by ℓ, and measuring how strong each one is.

origin: Greek monos, single, and polos, pole.

meanings.short: The simplest part of a distant object's field, depending only on its total charge or mass, as if all of it sat at one point.
meanings.long: It is the first term of the multipole expansion; its potential falls as 1/r. In general relativity a pure monopole is an idealised body with mass and nothing else: no size, no spin.

meanings.short: Short for magnetic monopole: a particle carrying a single magnetic pole, a north pole or a south pole on its own.
The third term of a multipole expansion: how a source is stretched or squashed, or the ℓ = 2 pattern over a sphere.
meanings.long: Its potential falls as 1/r³. It is set by a traceless symmetric tensor with two indices; two equal dipoles pointing opposite ways make a pure quadrupole. Gravitational waves are radiated by a changing mass quadrupole, and on the sky the quadrupole is the ℓ = 2 pattern of the CMB.

meanings.short: The fourth term of a multipole expansion, after the quadrupole; its potential falls as 1/r⁴.
meanings.long: It is set by a traceless symmetric tensor with three indices, the ℓ = 3 term. Its potential falls as 1/r⁴, so it matters only close to the source or when the lower terms vanish.

meanings.short: A solution in which a particle speeds up faster and faster with no outside force, a sign that the equation of motion is faulty.
meanings.long: With the Abraham–Lorentz force, an acceleration growing as e^(t/τ) solves the equation of motion with no outside force, where τ = 6.27 × 10⁻²⁴ s for an electron. Guth calls such solutions an error that comes from treating the charge as a point.

meanings.short: A quantity given by numbers with one or more indices, whose values change in a fixed way when the coordinates are rotated or changed.
meanings.long: A scalar has no index, a vector one, and an object such as the inertia tensor or the stress tensor two. Because every term of a tensor equation changes in the same way, an equation between tensors that holds in one coordinate system holds in all of them.

meanings.short: An arrow describing a surface: as long as its area and pointing straight out of it, added up piece by piece if it is curved.
meanings.long: For a wire loop, every surface bounded by the loop has the same vector area, half the loop integral of r × dℓ. The loop's magnetic dipole moment is the current times this vector area, whether the loop is flat or not.

meanings.short: Finding a force by imagining a tiny displacement that does not really happen and asking how much the energy would change.
meanings.long: If moving a surface by a small distance dx would change the stored energy by dW, with the charges held fixed, the force on it is −dW/dx. Guth uses it to find the outward pull on the surface of a charged conductor.

meanings.short: The work a force would do in an imagined small displacement that the constraints allow; constraint forces do none, which d'Alembert's principle uses.
Potentials in which the field here and now depends on what the sources will do later, so effects would come before causes.
meanings.long: They use the advanced time t + |r − r′|/c in place of the retarded time. They solve the same equations as the retarded potentials, but nature uses only the retarded ones: this is part of the arrow of time.

meanings.short: A time later than now by as long as light takes to cover the distance to the source: the opposite of the retarded time.
meanings.long: For a source point at distance d it is t + d/c. The advanced potentials are built with it; nature does not use them.

meanings.short: Potentials found by adding up every charge and current as it was at the retarded time, when its influence left at light speed.
meanings.long: In Lorenz gauge they solve the wave equations for V and A with sources: V is the sum of ρ/(4πε₀|r − r′|) with ρ taken at t − |r − r′|/c, and A is built the same way from the current. They express the fact that no influence travels faster than light.

meanings.short: Of two things being combined: swapping their order changes the sign of the result, as with the cross product.
meanings.long: The cross product is anticommutative: A × B = −B × A. Matrices A and B anticommute when AB = −BA; the Pauli matrices anticommute with each other, and Dirac needed four such matrices for his equation, which he found only as 4 × 4 matrices.

meanings.short: Of a product: spreading over a sum, so that a times (b + c) equals a times b plus a times c.
meanings.long: Ordinary multiplication, the dot product, the cross product and matrix multiplication are all distributive. Guth notes that a rival 'product' built from the sine of the angle would fail this test.

meanings.short: The magnetic field H, equal to B divided by μ₀ minus the magnetization; inside matter its curl is set by the free currents alone.
meanings.long: Splitting the current into free and bound parts and moving the bound part to the left of Ampère's law gives ∇ × H = J_free. In a linear material the magnetization is proportional to H.

meanings.short: The current that a magnetized material acts as if it carried, coming from its lined-up atomic magnets rather than from charges flowing through wires.
meanings.long: A magnetization M is equivalent to a current ∇ × M through the volume and a current M × n̂ on the surface. In a uniformly magnetized block the atomic loops cancel inside, leaving only the current around the surface.

meanings.short: A table of numbers giving the charge on each of several conductors from the potentials at which all of them are held.
meanings.long: Cᵢⱼ is the charge on conductor i when conductor j is held at unit potential and all the others at zero. Because electrostatics is linear, each charge is the sum of Cᵢⱼ times the potentials. The matrix is the inverse of the elastance matrix.

meanings.short: The inverse of the capacitance matrix: it gives the potential of each conductor from the charges on all of the conductors.
meanings.long: Pᵢⱼ is the potential of conductor i when conductor j carries unit charge and the others none. Guth remarks that the word elastance is seldom used.

meanings.short: Light given off when a charged particle moves through a material faster than light travels in that material, like an optical sonic boom.
meanings.long: The light leaves in a cone whose angle is set by the ratio of the two speeds. It is the blue glow in the water around nuclear reactors, and telescopes use it to detect very energetic particles from space.

meanings.short: A rearrangement that moves the first item of a list to the end: x, y, z becomes y, z, x, then z, x, y.
meanings.long: Cross products of unit vectors follow this pattern: from x̂ × ŷ = ẑ the cyclic permutations give ŷ × ẑ = x̂ and ẑ × x̂ = ŷ. Any list of three items has three cyclic permutations, counting the original order.

meanings.short: The wave operator, combining the Laplacian with the second time derivative over c²; a field it turns into zero obeys the wave equation.
meanings.long: It is written □² or □, and books differ on its overall sign: 8.07 uses ∇² − (1/c²)∂²/∂t², while 8.033 uses the opposite sign. It is the space-and-time version of the Laplacian and treats space and time alike, as relativity requires.

everyday: Not about wetness: here it means a motion dying away.

meanings.short: The gradual loss of energy from an oscillation or wave, by friction, resistance or radiation, so that its size dies away.
meanings.long: A damped oscillation has an amplitude that shrinks over time. Friction on a pendulum, resistance in a circuit and radiation from an accelerated charge all damp oscillations.

meanings.short: In 'damped Lyman-α system': a gas cloud so rich in hydrogen that its absorption line grows broad wings from the atom's natural damping.
The product of every second whole number down to 1 or 2, written with two exclamation marks, as in 5!! = 15.
meanings.long: So 5!! = 5 × 3 × 1 and 6!! = 6 × 4 × 2. (2ℓ − 1)!! equals (2ℓ)! divided by 2 to the power ℓ times ℓ!, and by convention (−1)!! = 1. It appears in the derivatives of 1/r and so in the multipole expansion.

meanings.short: Of a second-order partial differential equation: of the kind of Laplace's equation, where the solution at each point depends on the whole boundary at once.
meanings.long: If A, B and C are the coefficients of the second derivatives, the equation is elliptic when B² − 4AC < 0. Elliptic equations describe equilibrium: steady potentials, steady heat flow, stretched membranes.

meanings.short: Of a second-order partial differential equation: of the kind of the wave equation, where disturbances travel at a fixed speed.
meanings.long: If A, B and C are the coefficients of the second derivatives, the equation is hyperbolic when B² − 4AC > 0. It is named by analogy with the conic sections, as are parabolic and elliptic equations.

meanings.short: The statement that any reasonable wave or function can be built by adding up sine waves of different wavelengths.
meanings.long: A periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines (a Fourier series); any wave is an integral of complex exponentials e^(i(kz − ωt)) over the wave number (a Fourier transform). Guth notes that it is also called Dirichlet's theorem.

meanings.short: A dipole shrunk to zero size while its dipole moment is kept fixed, so that it has exactly the dipole field everywhere outside one point.
meanings.long: For an electric dipole the two charges move together as the charge grows; for a magnetic dipole a current loop shrinks as the current grows. The magnetic one keeps a delta-function term in its field at the origin, which gives hydrogen's 21 cm splitting. The same pattern appears in fluids: ideal flow past a sphere is a dipole flow outside it.

meanings.short: For radiation, assuming the source is much smaller than the wavelength it emits, so all its parts are seen at nearly the same phase.
meanings.long: It is the first term of an expansion in powers of the source size over the wavelength, the multipole expansion for radiation. 8.07 goes no further than this dipole term.

meanings.short: An imaginary charge placed inside a conductor so that, together with the real charges, it gives the right potential on the conductor's surface.
meanings.long: For a charge Q at height d above a grounded metal plane, an image −Q at depth d below it reproduces the field above the plane exactly. The image is a calculating device; the real charges are spread over the metal's surface.

meanings.short: A trick for problems with conductors: replace the conductor by imaginary charges chosen to give the right boundary values, then use their simple field.
meanings.long: It works because of the uniqueness theorem: once a guessed potential has the right sources and the right boundary values, it is the answer. It is practical only for simple surfaces such as a plane or a sphere.

meanings.short: How many times slower light travels in a material than in empty space, written n.
meanings.long: In a linear material n = √(με/(μ₀ε₀)), so light moves at c/n. When light passes from one material into another, n sets how much it bends (Snell's law) and how much is reflected.

meanings.short: The rule for the power radiated by an accelerated charge moving slowly: proportional to the square of its charge and the square of its acceleration.
meanings.long: P = μ₀q²a²/(6πc). Liénard's generalization extends it to any speed; for motion along a straight line it gains a factor γ⁶. It explains, for example, how a free electron scatters light (Thomson scattering).

meanings.short: The potentials of a single point charge moving on any path, found from the retarded potentials.
meanings.long: They are the Coulomb potential at the retarded time, divided by a factor 1 − n̂ · v/c that depends on the charge's velocity then. That factor is the surprise: a charge coming towards us counts for more. Differentiating them gives the fields of a moving charge, and from those radiation.

meanings.short: A material whose response to a field, its magnetization or polarization, is simply proportional to that field.
meanings.long: In a linear magnetic material M = χₘH, and in a linear dielectric P is proportional to E. Maxwell's equations inside such a material look like those of vacuum with μ₀ε₀ replaced by με.

meanings.short: The four equations that together describe all electric and magnetic fields: how charges and currents create them and how each changing field creates the other.
meanings.long: They are Gauss's law, Gauss's law for magnetism (no magnetic charges), Faraday's law and the Ampère–Maxwell law. Their solutions include electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light.

meanings.short: The one-way direction of real events, from past to future, although the basic laws of physics work equally well run backwards.
meanings.long: Radio signals arrive after they are sent, never before, and broken eggs do not reassemble. The most often heard explanation traces this to the very low entropy of the early universe; Guth finds it incomplete and suggests instead that the entropy of the universe may have no upper limit.

meanings.short: The region around a radiating source that is many wavelengths away, where the fields fall as 1/r and carry energy off for good.
meanings.long: Closer in, terms falling faster than 1/r dominate and the field looks like that of a static source. Only the 1/r part carries power to infinity.

meanings.short: The push back that a radiating charge feels from its own field, which removes the energy it radiates.
meanings.long: The Abraham–Lorentz force is the standard formula for it. It matches the radiated energy over a whole cycle but not at every instant, and it allows runaway solutions; Guth presents it as the place where classical electrodynamics reaches its limits.

meanings.short: In quantum field theory, a way of absorbing infinite quantities into the measured mass and charge so that every prediction comes out finite.
meanings.long: It is known to work at every step of the series in powers of the fine-structure constant, though the series as a whole is thought to diverge. Classically the same idea appears when the infinite self-energy of a point charge is absorbed into its measured mass.

meanings.short: Rescaled so that its probabilities add up to one again.
A formula that gives each Legendre polynomial by differentiating a power of x² − 1 the right number of times.
meanings.long: Pℓ(x) is 1/(2 to the power ℓ times ℓ!) times the ℓ-th derivative of (x² − 1) to the power ℓ. Similar formulas give other families of polynomials, such as the Hermite polynomials.

meanings.short: Being unchanged when everything involved is rotated together by the same rotation.
meanings.long: The dot product of two vectors is rotationally invariant: lengths and the angle between them do not change in a rotation. In quantum mechanics a rotationally invariant Hamiltonian commutes with every component of the angular momentum.

meanings.short: The energy a charge has from its own field, which becomes infinite if the charge is shrunk to a point.
meanings.long: For a ball of charge q and radius R it grows like q²/R. For point charges the self-energies are left out of the energy of a set of charges; the electron's finite mass shows that something beyond classical electrodynamics must take over at small distances.

meanings.short: Shaped like a sine curve: rising and falling smoothly and regularly, with a fixed wavelength or period.
meanings.long: A sinusoidal wave has the form A cos(kz − ωt + δ). By Fourier's theorem any wave can be built from sinusoidal ones.

meanings.short: The effective target area that a free electron presents to light it scatters, about 6.65 × 10⁻²⁹ square metres.
meanings.long: It is the scattered power divided by the intensity of the incoming wave, (8π/3) times the square of the classical electron radius, and it does not depend on frequency. It sets how often photons met free electrons in the early universe.

meanings.short: The theorem that, with the charges inside and the potential on the boundary given, Poisson's equation has only one solution.
meanings.long: For conductors, giving the total charge on each one also fixes the answer. Guth calls it a licence to guess: any potential that fits the equation and the boundary is the solution, however it was found.

meanings.short: The theorem that a differential equation with given starting values has exactly one solution.
meanings.long: For a second-order equation such as that of the oscillator, the starting position and velocity fix the solution, so any solution that fits them is the only one. So a solution found by guessing is the solution, once it fits the starting values.
